title: Bengal plans new cow-slaughter Bill and ₹1 lakh a year for cow shelters; four held in Murshidabad
dek: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said illegal slaughter would not be allowed and licensed slaughterhouses would not be touched. Police in Sagardighi made arrests the next morning.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
West Bengal will bring a new Bill to allow quick action against illegal cattle slaughter and will give registered cow shelters up to ₹1 lakh a year to look after old and sick cattle, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said after a cabinet meeting at the state secretariat, Nabanna, on Monday. Early on Tuesday police in Murshidabad district arrested four people they said were caught slaughtering an animal illegally.

"I will not allow the slaughter of cows in this state," Mr Adhikari told reporters. "We will bring a new Bill for quick action against offenders once information of illegal slaughter is received." He drew a line between unlawful slaughter and slaughter that is allowed under the law. "A slaughterhouse and the act of harming a cow are not the same thing," he said, according to reports. "If it is permitted in a slaughterhouse, you can do it."

## What the government announced

Until a new law is passed, the West Bengal Animal Slaughter Control Act, 1950, will remain in force, Mr Adhikari said. Under the Act, cattle may be slaughtered only if a designated veterinary officer certifies them fit for slaughter, which in the case of cows and calves is allowed only for animals over 14 years old or permanently unfit for work, and only in designated places, not in the open. "The power lies with veterinary surgeons," Mr Adhikari said. He also cited a Calcutta High Court order. No draft of the new Bill has been published, and he did not say whether it would come in the Assembly session that opens on 4 December.

The cabinet approved annual assistance of up to ₹1 lakh for the care and treatment of aged and abandoned cattle, under a programme the government is calling Gokul Mission, which reports linked to the Centre's Rashtriya Gokul Mission. Some reports said the grant would also be open to people who keep such cattle at home, and that the amount would depend on the number of animals. The Animal Resources Development department will issue detailed guidelines, according to reports. The scheme will also help buy milch cattle.

Mr Adhikari urged people to report covert slaughter. "If anything happens covertly, please inform me. Send me the details, and I will put a stop to it," he said. He cited recent police action in Howrah district, where he said four vehicles and about 550 kg of meat were seized and the accused remained in jail; reports differ slightly on the place name and the quantity.

## The Murshidabad arrests

Police from Sagardighi police station raided a secluded spot at Hajipur in the Sheikhdighi area before dawn on Tuesday on a tip-off and arrested four people, according to reports from the district. The meat was buried in accordance with procedure, the reports said. Police have not named the accused or said what charges they face, and are questioning them about where the meat was to be sold.

## Background

The state government invoked the 1950 Act in May, ahead of Eid, with restrictions on slaughter and on the buying and selling of cattle. Cattle smuggling across the Bangladesh border, much of it through Murshidabad, Malda and Nadia, has long been a political issue in Bengal. Bengal's 1950 law, unlike those in several BJP-ruled states, does not ban cow slaughter outright.

The announcement came at the same briefing at which Mr Adhikari said the cabinet had backed renaming the state "Paschim Banga". No reaction from the Trinamool Congress, now the main opposition, or from other parties had been reported by Tuesday afternoon.
